mainTopic: Why רבי יצחק says a finder who admits to part of a claim must take an oath: his view follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who holds that sometimes a person swears because of his own admission.
overview: The גמרא explains that רבי יצחק's ruling, that a finder who admits only part of what the owner claims must swear, follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. In a ברייתא, רבי אליעזר בן יעקב makes a borrower swear when he says, 'I owed your father a מנה and paid back part.' The חכמים say he is like a משיב אבידה and is exempt. To explain why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב doesn't exempt him, רב says the lender's heir made a claim. Since a קטן's claim has no legal weight, the גמרא explains that this 'קטן' is really an adult who knows little about his father's affairs. The גמרא tries to read 'his own claim' as 'others claim, but he admits'. It rejects that, because every partial-admission oath works that way. Finally, the גמרא explains the מחלוקת through רבה's teaching: a person won't brazenly deny a debt to his creditor's face, so the תורה adds an oath to push a staller to admit everything. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds the borrower is just as embarrassed before the lender's son, so he swears. The רבנן hold he would dare to deny to the son, so his partial admission is honest and he is exempt as a משיב אבידה.

steps.title: רבי יצחק follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יצחק holds like רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who teaches that a person can sometimes swear because of his own claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said his ruling following רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. A ברייתא teaches that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says there are times a person swears because of his own claim. How so? He says, 'I had a מנה of your father's, and I paid him back part of it.' He must swear. This is a case where a person swears on his own claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains where רבי יצחק's ruling about the finder comes from. It brings a ברייתא showing that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב also makes someone swear even when the only claim comes from his own mouth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a שבועה comes only when someone else makes a claim and the defendant admits part of it (מודה במקצת). רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says a borrower who brings up the debt himself and admits part of it must still swear about the rest. The finder in רבי יצחק's case works the same way, so he swears too.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
His own claim (his own statement, with no one else claiming)

steps.confusionAlert: On a first reading, nobody is suing the borrower. He brings up the debt himself, and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב still says he must swear. But in step 4 רב narrows the case: someone else, the lender's heir, did make a claim. Step 6 adds that this heir is an adult.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא דְּאָמַר, כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב –
phrases.english: He said it in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov —
phrases.notes: "He" is רבי יצחק, whose ruling about the finder was being questioned just before this.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: as it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:

phrases.aramaic: פְּעָמִים שֶׁאָדָם נִשְׁבָּע עַל טַעֲנַת עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: There are times when a person swears on his own claim.
How so?
"I had a maneh of your father's in my hand,
phrases.notes: He means he borrowed 100 זוז from the man's father, who has since died.

phrases.english: and I paid him back part of it" —
this person must swear.

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה הוּא שֶׁנִּשְׁבָּע עַל טַעֲנַת עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: And this is one who swears on his own claim.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא דְּאָמַר, כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier question about the source of רבי יצחק's ruling (from before this section).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the ruling to an earlier תנא's opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יצחק's ruling seemed to have no basis, because a finder is normally exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יצחק follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who says a person can swear on his own admission of part.

steps.title: The חכמים disagree: he is like one returning a lost object
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say the borrower who brings up the debt himself is like a משיב אבידה and does not swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the חכמים say: he is only like someone returning a lost object, and he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא gives the opposing view. The חכמים say this borrower is exempt from swearing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower could have stayed quiet and paid nothing, so his honesty is like returning a lost item. The חכמים do not want to punish honest people with a שבועה, so he is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: One who returns a lost object

phrases.english: But the Sages say:
he is only like one who returns a lost object,
and he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who admits a debt on his own, with no claim against him, is treated as a משיב אבידה and is exempt from a שבועה.

steps.title: Doesn't רבי אליעזר בן יעקב agree a returner of lost items is exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: does רבי אליעזר בן יעקב really reject the well-known rule that a משיב אבידה is exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: And does רבי אליעזר בן יעקב not hold that one who returns a lost object is exempt?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised. It seems strange that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב would reject the basic rule that a משיב אבידה does not swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption for a משיב אבידה is an accepted rule. It is hard to believe a תנא would disagree with it. So the גמרא pushes to understand his view differently.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב – לֵית לֵיהּ:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — does he not hold:
"One who returns a lost object is exempt"?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב לֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's position from Step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's ruling that the self-admitting borrower swears
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule 'משיב אבידה פטור' is accepted, so it is unlikely רבי אליעזר בן יעקב rejects it.

steps.title: רב: the case is where a minor made the claim
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב is talking about a case where a קטן, the heir, claimed the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: this is a case where a minor claims from him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers that the borrower did not bring up the debt completely on his own. The lender's young child claimed it from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is some claim against the borrower, so he is not purely a משיב אבידה. Since he admits only part, רבי אליעזר בן יעקב makes him swear. Everyone would agree he is exempt if nobody claimed at all.

phrases.english: Rav said: where a minor claims from him.
phrases.notes: The קטן is the lender's child who inherited the debt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 3 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower spoke completely on his own, so רבי אליעזר בן יעקב seemed to reject the משיב אבידה exemption.
steps.terutzMaskana: A minor made a claim, so the borrower is not a pure משיב אבידה, and he swears.

steps.title: A minor's claim has no legal weight
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב: a קטן's claim means nothing, as a משנה says no oath is taken on the claim of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does a minor's claim have any substance? Didn't we learn in a משנה: one does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's answer. A קטן's claim counts for nothing legally, so it should be as if nobody claimed at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משנה teaches that no שבועה is taken in response to a claim by a חרש, שוטה, or קטן. If the קטן's claim is worthless, the borrower is back to admitting on his own, which makes him a משיב אבידה again. So the original question returns.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn in a משנה
A deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor: people without legal competence

phrases.english: A minor — does he have any substance?!
phrases.notes: He means: does a minor's claim count for anything legally?

phrases.english: But didn't we learn:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל טַעֲנַת חֵרֵשׁ, שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן!
phrases.english: One does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor!
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in שבועות 38b.

steps.kashyaTarget: רב's explanation that a minor made the claim
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה rules that a קטן's claim does not require a שבועה. His claim counts as no claim, so the borrower should be exempt as a משיב אבידה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge puts the whole explanation of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, and with it רבי יצחק's source, back in question. The גמרא will need a better answer.

steps.title: The 'minor' is really an adult heir
steps.stepSummary: רב's 'קטן' means an adult son who is like a child about his father's business.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'minor' mean? An adult. Why call him a minor? Because about his father's affairs, he is like a minor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge against רב by saying the heir was really a grown-up. He is only called a 'קטן' because he does not know his father's business well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קשיא was that a real קטן's claim cannot lead to an oath. By making him a גדול, his claim counts in court. The word 'קטן' only describes how little he knows about his father's loans.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'קטן' here as a child in age. It means an adult who is a 'beginner' about his father's dealings.

phrases.english: What is meant by "minor"? An adult;
and why does he call him a "minor"?
Because regarding his father's affairs, he is a minor.
phrases.notes: He doesn't know for sure how much was repaid, so he is like a little kid about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5 by redefining 'קטן'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב meant an actual child, whose claim is worthless.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב meant an adult heir who is unfamiliar with his father's affairs.

steps.title: Then it is someone else's claim
steps.stepSummary: If the adult heir made the claim, why call it the borrower's own claim?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, is this 'his own claim'?! It is the claim of others!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new answer. If the heir is the one claiming, then the oath comes from someone else's claim, not the borrower's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said a person can swear 'על טענת עצמו'. But in רב's case the heir is the one making the claim. So the label 'his own claim' seems wrong.

phrases.english: If so, is it "his own claim"?!
It is the claim of others!

steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'טענת עצמו' used by רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an adult heir claims, the claim belongs to someone else, so the wording does not fit.

steps.title: Others claim, but he admits
steps.stepSummary: The claim is from others, but it is his own admission that makes him swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the claim of others, but his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'his own claim' really means his own admission. The heir claims, but the borrower's admission is what brings the oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heir only says 'I think you owe more'. What creates the oath is the borrower admitting part of the debt. So 'עצמו' points to the borrower's own words.

phrases.english: The claim of others, and his own admission.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'טענת עצמו' means the claim came from the borrower himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'טענת עצמו' means the oath comes from the borrower's own admission.

steps.title: Every oath case is like that
steps.stepSummary: Every מודה מקצת case is a claim by others plus one's own admission, so nothing is special here.
steps.simpleTranslation: All claims too are a claim of others and one's own admission!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the last answer. Every partial-admission oath works that way, so it cannot explain what is unique in this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In any מודה מקצת הטענה, the lender claims and the borrower admits part. If that is all רבי אליעזר בן יעקב meant, there would be no point in his special statement or a מחלוקת with the חכמים.

phrases.english: All claims too,
are the claim of others and one's own admission!

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That description fits every partial-admission case, so it cannot be what makes this case special.

steps.title: They argue about רבה's idea
steps.stepSummary: A new answer: the מחלוקת depends on רבה's teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they disagree about the teaching of רבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the earlier answer and offers a new one. This line is a setup: it tells us the argument depends on רבה, whose teaching is quoted next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of explaining the words 'טענת עצמו', the גמרא now looks for a deeper reason for the מחלוקת between רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים. The answer will rest on רבה's reason for the oath.

phrases.english: Rather, they disagree about the teaching of Rabba –

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer rejected in step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument was about the wording 'טענת עצמו'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument depends on רבה's reason for the oath of מודה מקצת.

steps.title: Why a partial admitter swears
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks why the תורה makes a מודה מקצת swear, and answers with a חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Why did the תורה say one who admits part of the claim must swear? Because of a presumption that a person is not brazen in front of his creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives the reason behind the oath of מודה מקצת הטענה. People don't have the nerve to deny a debt to the face of the person they owe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is: why should someone who admits part be worse off than someone who denies everything? רבה's answer starts with a חזקה about human behavior, which he explains further in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits part of the claim
A presumption about how people act

steps.whyThisMatters: This חזקה is the basic reasoning behind the whole oath of מודה מקצת הטענה.

phrases.english: As Rabba said:
For what reason did the Torah say
that one who admits part of the claim must swear?
There is a presumption: a person is not brazen
before his creditor;

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה, מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the teaching of רבה mentioned in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The oath of מודה מקצת is based on the חזקה that a person will not brazenly deny a debt to his creditor's face.

steps.title: He holds back only to stall
steps.stepSummary: The borrower would like to deny all but can't, and would like to admit all but is stalling, so the תורה adds an oath to push him to admit everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: This borrower wants to deny it all, but doesn't because a person is not brazen before his creditor. He really wants to admit it all, but he is stalling, thinking: until I have money and then I'll pay him. So the תורה said: put an oath on him, so that he will admit all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה finishes his explanation. The borrower who admits part is really stalling, and the oath is meant to push him to admit the full debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower is pulled two ways: he can't fully deny because of shame, and he holds back part only to buy time until he has money. Because he is basically honest but stalling, the threat of an oath should get him to admit everything.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה, a מודה מקצת is not a liar but a staller: he can't deny fully out of shame, and he holds back only for time. The oath is meant to get him to admit all. The גמרא is about to show how רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים disagree based on this.

phrases.english: And this one wants to deny all of it to him,
and the reason he did not deny it

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּאֵין אָדָם מֵעִיז פָּנָיו בִּפְנֵי בַּעַל חוֹבוֹ;
phrases.english: is because a person is not brazen before his creditor;
and he wants to admit all of it to him,
and the reason he did not admit it to him
is that he is putting him off –

phrases.aramaic: סָבַר: עַד דְּהָווּ לִי זוּזֵי וּפָרַעְנָא לֵיהּ;
phrases.english: he thinks: until I have money, and then I will pay him;
and the Merciful One said: Impose an oath on him,
so that he will admit all of it to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and explains רבה's חזקה from step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The partial admitter is stalling, not lying, so the תורה imposes an oath to push him to admit the full debt.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: The borrower is not brazen even toward the son
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds that a borrower wouldn't brazenly deny a debt to the lender or to the lender's son, so his partial admission is not like returning a lost item, and he must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds: it makes no difference whether it is the lender himself or his son. Either way, the borrower would not be brazen enough to deny everything. So he is not like someone returning a lost item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is using רבה's rule to explain why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב requires an oath. It says that in his view the borrower is just as embarrassed in front of the son as in front of the father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה taught that a borrower doesn't dare deny a debt completely to the lender's face. That is why the תורה adds an oath to push him to admit everything. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says this embarrassment applies to the son too. So the borrower's partial admission is not an act of honesty, and the regular oath of מודה מקצת applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Acts brazenly, has the nerve to deny outright
One who returns a lost item. Someone who admits what he could have hidden is treated as honest and exempt from an oath.

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'not brazen' leads to an oath, not an exemption. Because he would never have dared to deny it all, his partial admission proves nothing about his honesty.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds:

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא בּוֹ וְלָא שְׁנָא בִּבְנוֹ –
phrases.english: there is no difference between him and his son
phrases.notes: 'Him' means the lender. 'His son' is the lender's son, who is now making the claim.

phrases.english: he would not be brazen
and therefore he is not like one returning a lost item;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבה's rule from steps 11-12 to explain one side of the מחלוקת, as promised in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the מחלוקת as a disagreement about whether רבה's rule reaches the son
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed there was no clear basis for the disagreement
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב applies רבה's rule to the son as well, so an oath is required

steps.title: The רבנן: The borrower would be brazen toward the son, so admitting part is honest
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that the borrower would brazenly deny everything to the son. Since he admitted part anyway, he is like someone returning a lost item and is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן hold: he is only too embarrassed to deny in front of the lender himself. In front of the son he would have the nerve to deny. So since he did not deny, he is like someone returning a lost item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other side: the רבנן say רבה's rule only covers the lender himself, not his son. This finishes the explanation of the מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the רבנן, the borrower could easily have denied the whole debt to the son. When he chooses to admit part, he is being honest by his own choice. That makes him like a מֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה, who is exempt from an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Toward his son, meaning the lender's son

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides accept רבה's rule. They only argue about how far it reaches. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says the borrower is not brazen even toward the son, so he swears. The רבנן say he is brazen toward the son, so his partial admission is honest and he is exempt.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how one basic idea about human behavior can decide a legal outcome. The whole מחלוקת turns on a single question: who would a borrower dare to lie to?

phrases.english: And the Rabbis hold:
it is toward him that he is not brazen,
but toward his son he is brazen,
and since he was not brazen
phrases.notes: He could have denied it all to the son but didn't. Instead he admitted part.

phrases.english: he is like one returning a lost item.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the רבנן's side, completing the explanation of the מחלוקת started in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Completes the explanation of the מחלוקת based on רבה's rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Perhaps everyone applies רבה's rule equally to the son
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן limit רבה's rule to the lender himself, so the partial admission to the son counts as returning a lost item
